english: The dangers of every age have shown that respect for uncorrupted judgment flourishes among few people. Devoted to the pursuit of knowledge and eager for virtue, they can investigate the truth or dare to defend it once found. Or, as the apostle says, ‘They have their senses trained to distinguish good and evil’ (Hebrews 5:14). No storms of adversity break them, for they hear from the same teacher that they must resist sins to the point of shedding blood (Hebrews 12:4). These wise people, whom crowds of fools make appear few, therefore pursue knowledge and courage equally. Neither without the other attains either fruit or honor. Courage, unless directed by knowledge toward the best things, breaks out into contemptible madness. Conversely, the thoroughly tested laws of justice, unless enclosed by the wall of greatness of soul, will immediately lie open to plunder and be carried off into slavery to crimes. In different ages, therefore, very few have existed who cultivated, yoked, and drove this two-horse team, without which the world’s errors cannot be conquered. The pursuit of knowledge is impeded both by avoidance of labor and by the variety of worldly cares; steadfastness is shaken by fear of the troubles wicked people stir up. Faithful and wise minds indeed overcome these forms of assault. Yet they are so rare that among crowds of the insane they seem insane because they do not rage.

This is why the perseverance of the faithful, resisting the wickedness of the times and choosing ‘to suffer with God’s people rather than enjoy the passing pleasure of sin’ (Hebrews 11:25), is accused of stubbornness and contentiousness by those who say, ‘Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die’ (1 Corinthians 15:32; Isaiah 22:13) (Psalm 145:13, 17). Nothing is thought more consistent with prudent planning than buying the servitude of a degraded soul, or the unreliable peace of passing moments. It is chiefly this baseness of cowardly hearts that has allowed the filthy Manichaean doctrine to sail amid the churches’ shipwrecks. If a free and manly authority had stood firm in those exercising the priestly office, public agreement would have crushed the inventions of the advocates of inherited sin just as invincible reason overthrows them. But since lovers of present things value nothing less than religion, they have advanced into accusations against God. We have thus been forced to prove through such lengthy arguments that our God, who is the true God, is faithful in his words, just in his judgments, and holy in his works (Psalm 145:13, 17; LXX/Vulgate 144:13, 17).

english: The defender of natural evil attacks my books’ labor devoted to these matters. With what strength and how consistent an answer he does so, I have taught more than sufficiently in the preceding volumes’ discussion. I do not doubt that reading them makes this plain to every discerning person—the sort of person I have testified in this preface is rare: truth’s enemy strives only to make sport of simpler people’s ears, and thinks he has escaped if he merely appears to have answered somehow.

Although it is established that we have achieved this abundantly, our work nevertheless grows long. Let the wise reader understand that brevity was indeed desirable to us, but the needs of the case demanded that error spread more widely by the world’s favor be defeated by a broader battle line of truth. Our discourse therefore extends for a reason. With Christ’s help, I trust that no part of the impiety against which we contend will be judged carelessly investigated, insufficiently discovered, or only moderately battered. We therefore neither can nor should despair that, as time advances, the storm that has arisen may subside and the authority of the wise correct the cowardly crowd now making its uproar. But our wish matters less than our settled judgment. Whatever outcome the state of affairs receives, our grounds of goodwill and faith will stand. We do not depend on the outcome of popular success. We know the declaration of the three young men in Babylon. When a most arrogant king tried to compel them to worship a statue, they resisted with complete faithfulness, undeterred by the panting furnace lit to devour the devout. They answered as faith and steadfastness required: ‘Our God is able, O king, to free us from this furnace. But even if he does not free us, know that we do not worship your gods or adore the statue you have set up’ (Daniel 3:17–18). How reverently they mingled desire with judgment, without letting desire weaken the weight of their resolve! They neither cast faith’s courage down through despair nor suspend it on craving. They include their wishes, but do not abandon the proper order; they comfort endurance, but subordinate gentler outcomes to just ones. ‘It is certain,’ they say, ‘that our God can free us; whether he wills to do so is uncertain. Therefore, amid the uncertain outcome of events, the devout hold to a certain resolution: to reject idols and endure punishments. Let God consider what good our deliverance may bring to others. Meanwhile,’ they say, ‘let undefeated faith preserve our true happiness.’ One whose adversity trades for his glory has no excessive need to indulge easier outcomes. From this discipline left by illustrious teachers, we too understand that we must maintain moderation in our wishes for prosperity, but permanence in our decisions about the doctrines of faith. We desire, with the swelling of persecution restrained, to help the peoples too. But if that does not happen, our resolution stands: to endure every bitterness of insult and danger rather than fail to reject Manichaean filth and pollution.

But let us now approach the case. In both my earlier work and the present one, it has become clear that natural sexual desire, without which the union of the sexes cannot occur, was instituted by God, the creator of both human beings and animals (compare Augustine, Marriage and Desire 2.25). Even by my opponent’s admission, this is so decisive that natural sin cannot possibly be maintained without blaming that desire—bodily sexual desire—and slandering sexual union.

Since we have demonstrated this with the ability truth supplied, the discerning reader should have no further doubt about it. Wherever this appears in the writings of the advocate of inherited sin—who nevertheless cannot open his mouth without it—let it neither disturb listeners nor do anything except testify to its author’s shame. We will henceforth touch on it, if the matter compels us, with the brevity required. He attacks my statement: ‘This union of bodies, created by God with its heat, pleasure, and seed, is shown to be praiseworthy according to its own measure’ (Augustine, Marriage and Desire 2.25). But he passed over what I added: ‘Concerning something instituted by nature which sometimes also becomes a generous gift to the devout, even the devil does not dare to claim anything for himself with your effrontery.’

Passing over these points, then, he accuses me of not saying ‘with lust.’ He adds, as befits his doctrine’s sharpness: ‘The fruitful production of children is a gift to the devout, not the shameful union of bodily parts. A healthy nature would not have had this in begetting children, but that same nature, now corrupted, does have it. Consequently, the one born from it needs to be reborn’ (Augustine, Marriage and Desire 2.25). How consistent it all is! He calls children’s existence a gift to the devout, but places under the devil what he affirms God gives: the children. Sexual desire, however, which is in the shameful union of bodily parts, he calls diabolical. He does not deny its presence in the parents, yet acquits them of guilt. Would you say this man was born of a human being? What the parents do, he says, is diabolical, yet they are not guilty. What the children are by being born is God’s work, yet they are guilty. And he still thinks he has fought the demon rather than God! Those who think sin is natural thoroughly deserve to suffer this madness.

That Adam was to unite with his wife in no other way than the practice that developed is testified by the form of the organs, by God’s blessing pronounced no differently upon animals than upon human beings (Genesis 1:22, 28), and by the history itself, which shows bodily nature formed but does not declare it altered. Nothing against this universal testimony is found in God’s law—only in Mani’s books, which invent the claim that this sexual desire was poured in by the prince of darkness (Genesis 1:22) (Genesis 1:28).

english: By both our practice and our speech, we testify that everyone must be reborn through baptism. But this benefit is not bestowed so that people seem to have been kidnapped from the devil’s rightful possession. Rather, those who are God’s works become God’s children; those born in a lowly condition, but not a guilty one, are reborn at great worth, but without a false accusation. Those who come forth from God’s institutions are advanced by God’s mysteries; those who bring nature’s works receive grace’s gifts. Their Lord, who made them good by creating them, makes them better by renewing and adopting them. You must therefore confess that it is rightly said that the natural sin Mani invented, which you call original sin with a change of name, has perished. Nor does the catholic faith handed down from ancient times believe it: that faith does not doubt that infants are made by God and that nothing evil is made by him. Consequently, it does not pronounce God’s works guilty or place them under the devil’s jurisdiction, through a prejudgment against nature, before they exercise free will.

After this he passed over the whole continuous discussion of Abraham and Sarah, who received a son as a gift when their bodies were already as good as dead (Romans 4:19; Genesis 21:1–2). Even an ordinary reader, not only a wise one, understands how strongly their example supports the truth. He passed it over by saying it carried little weight against him. At least this statement, framed as follows, should have recalled him from such shamelessness: ‘To bring this argument’ (Romans 4:19)s main point to a brief conclusion: if the child whom God promised was given through sexual desire, then what fulfilled God’s pledge was undoubtedly good. english: This new natural philosopher therefore passes over those points and declares false what we said: ‘Just as the clay taken up at the beginning was the material of the human being, not his maker (Genesis 2:7), so now that power of pleasure which produces and mixes the seed does not perform the role of God’s activity. Rather, from nature’s storehouses it offers God the material from which he deigns to make a human being.’ He testifies that I said this correctly, except for my statement that seed is produced by the power of pleasure. He philosophizes as follows: ‘That pleasure of fleshly desire does not produce seed. The seed is already in bodies, created by the true God. It is not made by pleasure, but is stirred and emitted with pleasure’ (Augustine, Marriage and Desire 2.26).

He plainly said this not through fraud but through failure to understand. By ‘the power of pleasure’ I meant the very constitution of the male body, which I had to call virility. This virility—to use a word we have now made familiar—consists in the structure and health of the genitals and internal organs. It supplies the powers of both appetite and performance, and I called it the power of pleasure and desire. I preferred ‘power of pleasure’ to simply ‘pleasure’ precisely to indicate the whole ardor felt both before and during the act. Those disabled in their genital organs, namely eunuchs, do not possess seed, although certain embers of the extinguished fire still stir them. Because a particular disability has deprived them of the strength of the parts by whose service seed is produced from internal fluids, they are incapable of generation. God therefore established a power in the body which, unfolding at the proper time and provided health is present, reaches the capacity for fertility. Seed is consequently produced in bodies with the help of mature puberty. That is why premature pleasure stimulates the immature, but without the laws of age its kindling spark remains sterile.

That seed is mixed with pleasure, yet that one pleasure floats upon the senses while another lies deeper within the organs and closer to the result, is discussed at great length in medical writers. Hence even the Mantuan poet, more knowledgeable about nature than the Carthaginians’ little philosopher, notes that cattle should be made lean: when familiar pleasure first draws them toward mating, they should be kept from leafy fodder and springs. Often people shake them up by running and exhaust them in the sun, when the threshing floor groans under grain heavily pounded and light chaff is carried away on the breeze. This is done so that excessive abundance does not make the generative field less responsive or clog its sluggish furrows; instead the inner parts should experience a certain dryness, and thus thirstily seize the mating fluid and store it more deeply within (Virgil, Georgics 3.130–137). But it is enough to have noted the man’s sharpness even in these matters, which are not greatly needed for the case.

english: Yet everywhere I marvel at our debater’s consistency. He declares that seed is created by the true God, who also creates bodies, although it is emitted with pleasure. He therefore confesses that God makes the seed in which he says diabolical evil exists. And he is not ashamed to believe that God makes an evil to be imputed to the innocent.

Sexual desire, he says, has nothing to do with seed, because it was made by the devil. Married people serve this desire, while God makes seed and infants from seed. Yet the parents, who do the devil’s work, are neither guilty nor punished, he says. The infants whom God created, however, are assigned to crime and punishment. What the devil made—sexual desire—goes unpunished; it is thereby shown to be good, since it deserves no punishment. But what God makes is accused and condemned; it is thereby shown to be criminal, since not even respect for its maker can protect it from punishment. Divinity is to be believed to do something which even the most abject slavery could not endure. Such is the end of those who wage war on truth: they say nothing that is not impious and insane. Meanwhile, it is clear that no argument defends the innocent’s condition so well as the irreverence of their accusers does.

After this he tries to attack the point we established through the apostle Paul’s testimony: that God makes a human being from seed. He argues that I acted fraudulently by applying to this subject words admittedly spoken about grain. As though I had either broken the apostle’s statement in pieces there, as he imagines here, or recalled that testimony for any reason other than to demonstrate its conclusion: God must be believed to form every kind of seed. For after blessed Paul supported faith in the resurrection through examples of daily multiplication, he added something applicable to all nature: ‘But God gives it a body as he wills, and to each of the seeds its own body’ (1 Corinthians 15:38). That is, he assigns every seed the body its particular nature requires. I therefore did not intend words spoken about grain to be understood as about a human being. Rather, I seized upon the statement that God the maker gives each seed its own body to destroy your position, since your doctrine denies it. Therefore I certainly did not mention that statement needlessly, as you suppose, or use it fraudulently, as you falsely allege. Nor do you believe, despite your false oath, that God makes a human being from human seed. I affirm this not by conjecturing, but by understanding your creed.

english: What wise reader could hold back laughter on reaching the examples you next added? You say: ‘The apostle’s own words would refute this man, who bashfully names and shamelessly praises not a devout will but lustful pleasure. The very seeds farmers sow in the fields can refute him. Why should we not believe that God could have granted a blessed human being in paradise, concerning his own seed, what we see granted to farmers concerning wheat seed: that the former could be sown as the latter is, without any shameful lust?’ (Augustine, Marriage and Desire 2.14.29). How charmingly this bashful namer and shameless praiser makes utterly disorderly gestures and chants the songs of street entertainers!

But the other point cannot be read without great amusement: if Adam had not sinned, a woman could have been prepared for fertility like a crop field. Perhaps ears of children would burst out through every joint and through the tiny channels of the body which doctors call pores. Fertile in every part, she would sweat offspring instead of lice. But if some burst through her eyes, the mother would lose her sight; and if helmeted swarms emerged from the little globes of her pupils, blindness would undoubtedly pray for childlessness. Offspring not born but sweated out could easily be killed. We would thus have a race, like the Myrmidons in fables, but in Manichaean doctrine a race of lice or fleas. That would be the woman’s production. What could the man do? He would of course apply tools, not organs; deprived of genitals, he would drive in plowshares and hoes. The first human beings’ fault therefore deserves the fullest thanks, because it spared such a blessed nature these torments! Childbirth and a husband treat women more gently than if they felt plows or grew wild with importunate fertility all over their bodies.

‘Let the Manichaeans’ faces be filled with disgrace, and let them seek your name, Lord’ (adapted from Psalm 83:16; LXX/Vulgate 82:17). What monstrous accusers of the innocent and God! What support from arguments and testimonies! ‘Why,’ he asks, ‘should we not believe nature could have been made differently from what we see?’ (Psalm 83:16) As though the question were what God could have done rather than what he established! If this lust for conjecture entitles us to criticize what was made—saying that because things could have been made differently, their actual arrangements do not testify to a good nature—let us declare that God could have made mortals two-headed. Therefore one-headed people who stand on their feet were badly made: they could have been given a head at each end. This shape sometimes appears in little worms, whose belly is enclosed by a head at both ends, so that they begin from either shoulder and are understood to end in the middle. Admit these absurdities, and where will delirium stop?

God, then, could have made human beings sprout from the earth with flowers. As far as his power goes, I do not deny he could. But he willed them to be born only from the sexes. We are asking what he did, not what he could do. On this point it is a mad answer to say: ‘What exists is evil because God could have done it differently.’ (adapted from Psalm 83:16) This is to praise God as an insult to himself and proclaim his almighty power as a stain upon his judgment. It is not praise at all, but a great insult, to give to his strength what you take away from his wisdom and say that God possessed power but lacked good judgment. Criticism of his judgment reaches directly into denial of his power: he cannot do everything if he cannot arrange things well. Indeed, if he falls short of supreme wisdom, he retains no claim to reverence as God. Since even to suspect this is utterly impious, we return to the point that cuts your doctrine of inherited transmission’s throat. God, who made everything very good, established nothing in such a way that it can be proved that, within the kind actually made, it could have been made more suitably or reasonably (Genesis 1:31). Equally endowed with wisdom and almighty power, he would not establish something a mere little man could rightly criticize. Whatever is shown to be natural in all creatures whatsoever was therefore made so excellently that a proposed correction of it is shown foolish and impious.

The shape of a horse and the shape of an ox differ when compared with each other. Yet within their own kinds they have received a harmony so suitable in every respect that neither horse nor ox should or could have been established differently from the form we see. This rule can be applied to everything swimming, crawling, walking, or flying, and finally to things of the upper air and heavens: no creature’s form can be proved capable of being better established for the kind for which it was prepared. So too the human being, already included above among walking creatures, is formed throughout in a way no one could improve. Wisely, the human body received both parts for display and parts for modest concealment, so that a person would learn both modesty and confidence within himself. He would look misshapen if veiled all over, but would become idle and careless if always exposed all over. Human fertility therefore should have received no organs in either sex other than those it has, no other arrangement of internal parts, no other sensations, and no other pleasure.

Let us therefore warn the Manichaeans to stop criticizing the works of divine wisdom and correct their own perverse opinions. Saying that human beings would have reproduced differently from the way universal experience attests does not concern the question. Both reason and Scripture testify that they could not have been made better than they were: Scripture proclaims that God made everything not merely good but very good (Genesis 1:31; Sirach 39:16, Latin numbering 39:21). Thus here too, as throughout the whole work, the Manichaeans’ doctrine has collapsed. We do confess that in the future the blessed will have more glorious bodies needing no assistance. But this too was excellently established by the most just and wise God: nature should not displace the condition belonging to reward. There should be a first stage in which natural freedom stands and from which, by the right of free will, a person either descends to the depths of punishment or strives toward the summit of glory by the paths God established.

english: Since enough has been said about this, let us hasten to the arguments Mani once cleverly advanced concerning natural evil—although, as I shall prove, he was deceived by tangled questions. First, however, let us briefly examine what Augustine replied to the apostle’s testimony. I had said that blessed Paul’s testimony proved most clearly that God, the creator of bodies, instituted the familiar activity of the sexes. Denouncing the shameful acts of those whose madness had plunged them even into intercourse with the male sex, Paul says: ‘Abandoning the natural use of the female, they burned in their own desires’ (Romans 1:27). I inferred, with the apostle as witness, that intercourse with the female is shown to have been naturally instituted.

In response this man writes: ‘The apostle did not say “marital use” but “natural use.” He meant that which takes place with organs created so that the two sexes can unite through them for generation. Consequently, when someone unites with a prostitute using the same organs, it is natural use, yet not praiseworthy but blameworthy. This term, “natural use,” therefore did not praise marital union. It identified acts more unclean and criminal than if they had used women unlawfully but nevertheless naturally’ (Augustine, Marriage and Desire 2.20.35). That is: this intercourse with the female which the apostle called natural is not understood as marital, so as to be shown good and lawful. Rather, he says, it is called natural because it indicates that the difference of sex was instituted to prepare both for union and for birth. Since these exertions gained him nothing, why did he spend so long on them? Certainly only so that his followers might think a point answered merely because they saw it touched. A brief argument will show how he said nothing. The apostle says intercourse with the female was naturally instituted; he did not commend some different union originally ordained. Discussing the intercourse in which he knew sexual desire had flourished at every period, he called it natural.

This is what we understood. Speaking about nature’s institution, we brought forward what the apostle plainly meant. What, then, did you accomplish by replying that he calls it natural rather than marital use? Or with what mouth do you add: ‘When someone unites with a prostitute using the same organs, it is natural use, yet not praiseworthy but blameworthy’ (Romans 1:27)? Let us show here too what we have often disclosed: you utter not even one sentence that does not count strongly against you. If the use involved in fornication is called natural, yet not praiseworthy but blameworthy because it is intercourse with a prostitute, you will undoubtedly confess marital intercourse, because it is honorable and lawful, to be not blameworthy but praiseworthy (compare Romans 1:27).

english: Where, then, is your diabolical crime, which you tried to attach to it through the argument from shame? Sexual desire itself is no longer being condemned—the desire felt by nature’s own constitution in both forbidden and permitted intercourse—if only its distortion, straying toward what is unlawful, is blamed.

To ask closely and briefly: when the apostle Paul called it the natural use of the female, do you think he indicated both its possibility and its propriety, or only its possibility? In other words, by ‘natural’ did he mean an act that could and should occur, or one that could occur but should not? If you say, ‘One that could occur, although it should not,’ (Romans 1:27) as happens in adultery, then that other shameful act will not be contrary to nature either, since it is performed with natural organs. But if, recoiling in alarm, you reply with the truth—that the apostle called natural an act directed toward offspring, which could and should be performed honorably because naturally, with the bodies of one woman or several as permitted according to the circumstances of the time—you will undoubtedly confess your argument foolish. By ‘natural use,’ blessed Paul indicated not fornication, as you thought, but the honorable and legitimate union of bodies arranged for fertility.

We therefore rightly defend in general what the Manichaean accused in general. You say this pleasurable union of the sexes was instituted by the devil, is the cause of original sin, and necessitates all crimes. You thus accuse nature itself. What could we more consistently have done than, with the Teacher of the Gentiles as witness, defend on the general ground of nature, and assign to God’s work, what you called naturally evil? Thus, to refute you, we proved that what you call diabolical was naturally instituted. This is the proper and learned way to answer: defend in particular what is accused in particular, and vindicate in general what is accused in general. Mani understood this too. You equal him in crime but not in intelligence. That is why he assigns the whole substance of bodies to the devil; you assign not all of it but, as we said in the preceding book, the better part. Truth has therefore triumphed, surrounded by sacred defenses. Proving through the apostle that married people’s activity is natural, and therefore belongs to God as nature’s creator, it has shattered the inventions of you who swear it comes from transgression, not nature (compare Romans 1:27).

english: With similar sharpness you also try to undermine my use of the Gospel testimony that a tree must be known by its fruits. I used it to demonstrate the obvious: marriage cannot be shown good—nor, indeed, the nature replenished through marital activity—or vindicated as God’s work if crimes are said to sprout from it. You replied: ‘Was the Lord speaking about that, rather than about two human wills, the good and the evil? He called the former a good tree and the latter an evil tree, because good works arise from a good will and evil works from an evil one. If we understand marriage as a good tree, we must certainly place fornication opposite it as an evil tree. But if he says that adultery should not be put in the tree’ (John 8:48)s place there, but rather the human nature from which a human being is born, then here too the tree will not be marriage but the human nature from which a human being is born’ (Augustine, Marriage and Desire 2.26.43).

You are mistaken. The Lord is speaking there not about two wills but about his own person. Although he conferred countless benefits on the Jews, they never stopped accusing him. They could not condemn his works, which they even glorified; nevertheless they charged him with being a Samaritan, full of a demon, and deceiving them by Beelzebul’s spirit (John 8:48; Matthew 12:24). Then the Lord said: ‘Either make the tree good and its fruits good, or make the tree evil and its fruits evil; for a tree is recognized by its fruits’ (Matthew 12:33) (Matthew 12:24). That is: either criticize my works, whose goodness is attested by illnesses driven away and health restored, so that you establish my wickedness from the evidence of my works; or, if you do not dare condemn these great benefits, give the good tree—that is, me—the testimony of my fruits. You who praise the benefits must love the benefactor. There, then, Christ commanded that a person be recognized from his works. This rightly supported our teaching that nature and marriage too must be assessed from the quality of their fruitfulness. If the poison of crimes flowed from them, the root too should be judged criminal.

See how blind your understanding is. You thought you could lighten my objection’s weight by placing fornication opposite marriage, so that marriage would appear a good tree and fornication an evil one. Then no fertility should arise from fornication, lest it be proved evil if good marriage were proved by good offspring. But whether a human being is born from marriage or adultery, he proceeds not from shameful conduct but from the nature of seed. The shameful act committed by adulterers’ will does not disturb the arrangements of substance. Nature exercises itself through its own materials. The sin remains with the author of the unlawful will, while innocent offspring comes forth through the creator’s work. You too saw that this answer had to be given. But let the discerning reader attend to how you tried to evade it.

You say: ‘If adultery is not to be placed in the tree’s position there, but human nature from which a human being is born, then here too the good tree will not be marriage but human nature from which a human being is born.’ Here, then, is what you tried to express: just as a human being is not attributed to fornication but to nature, so the sin derived from lawful parents should not be attributed to marriage but to human nature, which the devil infected with an ancient crime. In adulterers, then, you blamed the wanton people’s will, but praised human nature, from which a human being was born even through unlawful intercourse. In lawful parents, however, you praised marriage, from which you deny sin comes, but criticized nature, from which you say a dreadful crime is poured forth.

Let my reader be alert here. If you judged human nature praiseworthy in fornication because it provided the newborn child’s origin unstained by the partners’ shameful acts, how do you condemn that same nature in marriage, saying it provided the cause of natural guilt? You have therefore professed not marriage but human nature to be both a great good and a great evil. What could be more wicked than it, if it engendered crime? What more detestable, if it is possessed by the devil? Let nature attend to whatever skill it has in seed. For the moment, in its quality—the sphere to which every good or evil belongs—it is proved utterly evil if it is itself guilty, produces guilt, and is convicted as the servant of diabolical tyranny. Rightly, then, a tree must be known by its fruits, so that what causes evil is most rightly called evil.

english: But we speak this way to show where your creed ends. The point founded by the preceding discussions remains unshaken: nothing is evil except the act of a will committing what justice forbids; nor can what is natural be proved evil. This tower therefore stands unshaken, and from its height the brigandage of different errors is repelled.

Let us now pursue what the passage requires. It is clear, most subtle debater, that you have exalted one and the same thing—human nature—with great praises, but stained it with still greater accusations. Just as these cannot occur together at one time, in one work, and under one intention, so natural reason cannot admit them even as alternating opposites. Nature always possesses one full valuation, namely goodness. It is never attacked for evil—which its institutions, because of its maker’s dignity, do not admit—except by the utterly filthy teeth of the Manichaeans.

Having completed this point, I ask what wisps of marriage you think you should pursue. If you confess that the cause of a human being is not marriage but nature, and the cause of sin too is not marriage but nature, then the marriage you were praising has entirely vanished. To what effect is it assigned if it is the cause of neither your evil nor my good? You remove the human being from marriage’s honorable activity lest you be compelled to attribute him to fornication too. You remove sin from marriage’s necessary activity lest you appear to condemn marriage. What remains worthy of praise in marriage’s possession? Why fear to violate with a word what you have utterly demolished by argument? Of what will it be called the cause if it shares in neither natural evil nor natural good? Do the name and honor of marriage now accomplish nothing in human affairs?

But you are choking, and painfully. We must therefore help the panting old man. Something remains you can give marriage, without which nothing else is found: say that marriage stands guard at the door, allowing no report of obscenity to burst in upon the partners’ pleasure, but claiming honor and modesty for that activity under its own title. Your attempt to corrupt marriage’s integrity with deceitful praise was therefore pointless. It is more hostile to no one than to you. It drives you utterly away and does not allow Manichaean tongues to creep in and lacerate the union entrusted to its protection. ‘They have brothels worthy of their doctrine,’ it says, ‘where they may satisfy themselves at night.’ Marriage’s watch guards the pleasure of modest people; crimes are barred and the honor of decency admitted. The privileges the apostle granted defend honorable marriage and undefiled beds; ‘but God will judge fornicators and adulterers’ (Hebrews 13:4). Where, then, is the criminal union, if the authority of the marriage you praised serves its activity and privacy?

With these matters resolved, I will briefly show how deeply you lie in ignorance, although until now you were considered most subtle and acute. You say you attribute to nature, not marriage, the crime that passes to offspring, just as, on the other side, you attribute human beings to nature, not to a shameful act. You therefore pretend to praise marriage, to avoid being openly detected as a Manichaean, while criticizing nature, in which you confess evil exists and from which evil is propagated. Could you never hear the rules of argument and the principles of thoroughly sound reason? In every category, genera encompass more than species; subordinate genera also arise in this way. Species encompass more than individuals. Genera contain species, and the lowest species contain individuals. Shaking the lower things, then, does not shake the higher; but the higher things, by their own collapse, carry down everything they encompassed.

For example, ‘animal’ is a genus. In the breadth of its meaning it includes different species, such as human being, horse, ox, and others. If one species perishes, the genus does not suffer destruction. Suppose the nature of oxen disappears from existence: the genus is certainly not destroyed, since the nature of other animals remains. Conversely, if what ‘animal’ means is removed from existence, every species included under that genus undoubtedly perishes. No species of animate creature will remain once animal life is entirely destroyed. The higher things therefore share their fortunes and characteristics with the species they encompass. The reverse does not occur: the higher are not altered by the variations of their species as though by binding relationships.

To apply the example to the case: human nature in its generality is a kind of genus for the arrangements situated within it. It has, as it were, species in bodily position, organs, orders, movements, and other such things. It therefore shares its quality with all its subordinate species, but does not bind itself so as to share the risks of things lower than itself. If nature, then, is condemned and believed guilty and subject to the devil, marriage beneath it, fertility, and the whole substance will also be condemned. Marriage, which follows nature, cannot therefore be praised if nature itself is criticized. The beauty of severed shoots must die together with its root. To put the thing more plainly: the business of marriage cannot be called good if natural union is accused, since what is devalued in the genus to which it inseparably belongs cannot be honored in the species.

But when an evil will uses natural instruments for shameful acts, that power of pleasure and seed—which never varies according to the partners’ will—shares no part in the crime. It supplies material to God as he works, and the shameful act condemns only the adulterer’s deserving conduct, not nature’s. Since we were discussing natural things, your condemnation of nature alongside praise of marriage was exceedingly dull-witted. It is irrefutably established that a genus shares whatever it receives with its species. Therefore either the use the apostle calls natural will be judged good and legitimate, marriages will be honorable, and there will be no natural sin; or, if nature is believed diabolical so that original sin can exist, marital intercourse too will be declared condemnable. This is to embrace the Manichaeans’ doctrine, not soberly, but openly. Since that doctrine is deadly, and they possess nothing of truth, honor, or faith, while the theory of natural sin can belong to no others, it is established that we are catholics and you Manichaeans (compare Romans 1:27) (Romans 1:27).

english: To avoid the odium of this name, your mention of various heresies is entirely futile. You say: ‘Just as Arians call catholics Sabellians, although catholics distinguish the persons clearly while preserving their common nature, so you impose the Manichaeans’ name on us, although we do not say marriage is evil, as Manichaeans do, but say evil passes into all human beings as a condition of nature’ (Augustine, Marriage and Desire 2.23.38). I have no doubt the wise will laugh at these arguments. Arians falsely call catholics Sabellians, since we distinguish the persons of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit without any confusion or change of substance, while they very stupidly slander us as though one and three were no different. Likewise, catholics most rightly declare you Manichaeans, because your creed compels us to say so.

Manichaeans assert natural sin; you say it is natural. They say the devil planted bodily desire; you confirm this through extended argument. They contend that evil cannot be avoided through free will because it is natural. With the same words you too invent a free will through which evil can be done, but evil cannot be abandoned. Mani says seed is cursed; you try to prove it by scriptural authority. Mani says wickedness cannot be changed; you shout that it is so. But you say Adam alone possessed a better nature. Mani too, writing to Patricius, says Adam should be believed better than those who followed, as though formed from the flower of the first substance. You say intercourse is diabolical because of its natural movements, and human beings are rightly plucked by the devil like fruit from a shrub he planted. Mani says this too: he is, indeed, the one from whom you learned to believe and affirm it. Mani says both nature and marriage are evil. You say marriage is good but nature guilty. You are not more religious here; he is more intelligent.

Just as it is false when Arians say catholics are Sabellians, then, it is entirely true when catholics say advocates of inherited sin are nothing other than Manichaeans. The illusory distinction between you arises not from your creed but from your ignorance. You and Mani therefore hold one faith, but he proves less shameless than your distinguished self. For one does not readily meet either a Manichaean or another Melitides who says he condemns human nature without slandering marriage.

english: But enough has been said against these absurdities. Let us come to the exceedingly tangled question I mentioned above, whose subtlety deceived your teacher himself. You tried to meet our objection not by explaining it but by putting forward another, more difficult one. I had taught that in adults who work evil by their own will, nature’s innocent beginnings are praised while the deviations of their actions are rightly blamed. There are two things, therefore, to which opposite judgments can apply. In infants, however, there is only one thing, nature, since there is no will. That one thing must be reckoned either to God or to the demon. I concluded that, if nature exists through God, original evil cannot be within it; but if nature is transferred to the devil through inborn evil, nothing remains by which the human being can be vindicated as God’s work. When you reached these passages, you replied with your usual good faith that my conclusion was true, but that infants too have two things: nature and sin. Yet sin, to recall the previous definitions, is nothing other than the will to retain or commit what justice forbids and from which one is free to abstain. With sin thus established as nothing other than the choice of an evil will, you replied, Epicurus of our age, that infants possess sin but no will. How disgraceful that is, the fourth book has already shown.

In these passages I said, ‘If sin comes from will, the will producing sin is evil; if from nature, the nature producing sin is evil.’ You tried to confront me with a question plainly not invented by you. Some years ago, when we were in Carthage, a certain Honoratus, a friend of yours and equally a Manichaean—as your letters indicate—put this same question to me. I mention this only to make clear that this is the question which deceived Mani and Marcion so many centuries ago. Against my statement, ‘If sin lies in nature, the nature producing sin is evil,’ you speak as follows:

‘I ask him to answer if he can. Just as plainly all evil deeds arise as fruits from an evil will as from an evil tree, so whence does he say the evil will itself arose—the evil tree bearing evil fruits? If from an angel, what was that angel but God’s good work? If from a human being, what was that human being but God’s good work? Rather, since the angel’s evil will arose from the angel, and the human being’s from the human being, what were these two before those evils arose within them, except God’s good work and a good and praiseworthy nature? See, then: evil arises from good, and there was absolutely nothing from which it could arise except good. I mean the evil will itself, preceded by no evil—not evil works, which arise only from an evil will as from an evil tree. Yet the evil will could arise from good not because the good was made by the good God, but because it was made from nothing, not from God. Why, then, does he say: “If nature is God’s work, the devil’s work is not permitted to pass through God’s work”? Did not the devil’s work, when it first arose in the angel who became the devil, arise in God’s work? Therefore, if an evil that existed nowhere could arise in God’s work, why could an evil already existing somewhere not pass through God’s work? Are human beings not God’s work? Sin therefore passed through human beings—that is, the devil’s work through God’s work. To say the same thing another way: the work of God’s work through God’s work’ (Augustine, Marriage and Desire 2.28.48).

These many words I have quoted from you have fully disclosed the very head and fountain of the ancient error. You have offered nothing sharper in your statements, nothing more intricate in argument. Driven across the whole field of debate, and expelled by hostile truth’s weapons from every place where you tried to stand, you have at last reached the cave Mani dug among the shadows of difficult questions. You testified to this question’s difficulty by saying, ‘I ask him to answer if he can.’ Since we both agree that the point is difficult, I urge the reader to attend with his whole mind. Let him follow the distinctions, subtle as the matter requires—distinctions which I trust Christ’s help will make substantial—first attentively and then confidently. You asked, then, where evil comes from. I ask what evil you mean, since this name is shared by guilt and punishment. Punishment, however, is called evil only in an extended sense, since the gravity of the judgment imposing it justifies it. You reply that you mean sin, not punishment.
translator_notes: The online Latin in this quotation reads “God’s work through the work of God’s work.” The translation restores the order “the work of God’s work through God’s work,” which Augustine gives when repeating this same passage at 5.63. His point is that the devil, as a created angel, is himself God’s work; sin is that creature’s work.

english: You therefore ask where this evil comes from which rightly deserves the name evil: sin. I reply that it is exceedingly unskilled to ask the origin of something whose definition has not yet been established. Let us first see whether it exists, then what it is, and last where it comes from. I did this in the first book of the present work, but there I proceeded with some points already secure. Let us now question whether evil exists.

Repeated vices and severe judgments testify that it does. It is therefore established that sin exists. We ask what it is: whether it is some body visibly composed of many elements, or some single thing, like one element considered in thought apart from its combination with the others. But it is none of these. What is it, then? An appetite of free will which justice prohibits. Or, to use the earlier definition: the will to do what justice forbids and from which one is free to abstain. Consider, then, whether sin can be found outside the boundaries of this definition, lest what we suppose contained be wandering elsewhere. Let us consult the judge’s justice, so that its testimony too may establish whether every kind of sin has been properly enclosed by these limits.

Does God impute what he knows cannot be avoided? That would be no justice, but the greatest disgrace. Indeed, if this occurred, sins would not be punished but increased. A just judge ordinarily punishes guilt. If guilt invaded the judge himself through the corruption of justice, it would have taken vengeance upon the judge, not been punished. Justice therefore imputes nothing as sin except what one is free to avoid. But nothing can be called free unless, without any unavoidable compulsion of natural forces, it lies within the authority of a will possessing its own freedom. The definition is therefore excellent and complete: sin is the will to do what justice forbids and from which one is free to abstain. With these points resolved, let us ask where it comes from—a question asked in great disorder before these definitions. Where, then, does sin come from? I answer: from the doer’s free will.

Let us see, however, whether what the preceding definition established is confirmed by everyone’s agreement. Certainly no wise person or catholic can doubt this: nothing is sin except what can be avoided, and no justice exists except that which charges a person with what he himself committed by free will, although he could have avoided it.

These points no longer slip from our grasp, but the Manichaean and the advocate of inherited sin reject them with equal determination. Let us see, then, what they themselves say. Mani writes that sin is natural. Augustine agrees that sin is natural. Both therefore dissent from the definition we gave, and form an association in calling sin natural. Let us also see what they say about the kind of sin—what they regard as the sin both affirm to be natural—lest perhaps they disagree at the next step. What does Mani write to his daughter? That fleshly desire, and the pleasure appointed for the work of fertility, is proved diabolical because its act avoids public view. What does Augustine say? Exactly the same: ‘That fleshly desire is the devil’s shrub, the cause and law of sin, which everywhere avoids observation and seeks privacy through shame’ (Augustine, Marriage and Desire 1.7.8; 1.23.26). Thus they differ neither in their first nor their second account of evil.

What is the third point? When asked where evil comes from, Mani says, ‘From the eternal nature of darkness.’ What does Augustine say? ‘My teacher goes too far in thinking evil never began. It began through the first man’s will—or rather, already through the will of a higher nature, the angelic—but from that time it became natural.’ His teacher naturally beats him and drags him to court with great authority. How will a catholic judge between them? Mani is undoubtedly exceedingly foolish in thinking sin natural; but compared with Augustine’s intelligence, he looks very acute. They agree that sin is natural, confess that this sin is of one kind, and think it possesses the entire human race. Yet afterward the pupil dares to say that in one person alone it was not natural, although he confesses it innate in everyone else! After disgracing him with a schoolboy’s beating, they will place him under his teacher, whose blasphemy is more consistent. But they will expel both pupil and teacher together from the assembly of the devout. See, then, what we allow you. You dislike Mani’s statement that evil is natural. Say, then, that no one is born guilty, and you have escaped—by denying original sin, of course. But you do not say this. You therefore confess that you wish neither to leave your teacher nor to join the catholics.

You thought it a powerful objection to ask where an evil will arose in the first man himself, or in the devil who had been created an angel. Yet you say it arose in God’s work—that is, in an angel or a human being—not because he was God’s work, but because he was made from nothing. Take care, then, that by different paths you too do not say the necessity of evil was eternal. If the cause of evil’s arising in God’s work was that the work had admittedly been made from nothing, then before what exists was made, this nothing always was. That is, before what exists was made, nothing had ever existed; what never existed is said to have been nothing. From eternity, therefore, what did not exist before being made by God—whose substance alone has no beginning—never existed. This emptiness, then, this nothing, always was before the existence of things brought it to an end. This nothing was not made; creatures were made, and the nothing ceased to be.

In a creature made from nothing, however, you invent the claim that evil arose precisely because it was made from nothing. You have therefore attributed the evil arising in a human being to his origin; and you say that origin—nothing—was sin’s cause. For you say: ‘Evil arose in a human being not because he had been made by God, but because he had been made from nothing.’ If evil therefore arose because the condition of the preceding nothing required it, and that nothing was eternal, you have fallen by altered paths and now hang entirely in your teacher’s snare: both of you confess evil to be from eternity. But here too he is more intelligent. Introducing natural sin, he said an eternal substance of darkness existed which compelled this evil to be present without the sinner’s will. He therefore gave an author to the thing he made necessary, so that the evil invading substances would appear to have something forcing it. You, however, with the unbearable leadenness of your mind, affirm the necessity of evil but deny an author of that necessity. As with infants, so with the very first doer of sin, you leave the deed in place, and say that some great mystery can be understood: that this nothing had immense power, although it was nothing.

For you affirm that this nothing, from which all things were made, was sin’s cause. The power of this nothing therefore accomplishes as much for you as the prince of darkness does for Mani. Both of you say that even the first evil arose by necessity. But he supplies something solid, although evil; you supply emptiness, equally evil. He therefore says there is a violent substance; you say there is something equally violent, but nothing. See, then, the conclusion of your syllogism. When nothing had yet been created, ‘nothing’ indicated eternal emptiness. But this very nothing—that is, emptiness—was brought to an end when creatures arose: it ceased to be nothing when something began to be. Thus even when this nothing was, it was not, since it is understood to have been only when nothing yet existed. After things were made, this indication of emptiness—nothing—lost even its name, just as it had never possessed substance. Thus what had never existed in reality lost even its name. You invent the claim that by its violence evil arose in both angel and human being. What could be more insane?

You say that a thing which did not exist possessed great power for the sole reason that it had never existed, but that it began to have immense power just when it lost even its name. This nothing gained a great dominion after even its designation had perished!

Well done for your mighty wisdom! By the rules of a new method of argument first invented by you, you embrace conclusions by denying their premises, and assemble bodies severed from their heads. We do not envy your subtleties. Rather, with Christian kindness we pity you: you have found an ending worthy of your doctrine, departing from accusations against the innocent and arriving at nothing.

What soundness! What elegance in a debater! ‘Evil arose in a human being,’ he says, ‘not because he was made by God, but because he was made from nothing’ (Augustine, Marriage and Desire 2.28.48). We have already shown the sharpness by which immense power is assigned to this nothing. Now I point out what the preceding debate also made clear: not even the first evil was undertaken by the sinner’s will if the condition of an origin from nothing required its birth.

You have therefore supplied a nature for even the first evil, emptier than Mani’s, but equally eternal. There is no need to fight further about this. It is entirely clear that a pact remains between you, bound by the chain of natural and eternal evil.

I have certainly proceeded as the honesty of debate required. Careful investigation by reason has crushed what your argument established: that the evil will arose in God’s work because the human being had been created from nothing. It has shown that, with changed terms, you said the same thing Mani invented and believed: that the first sin too was generated by the violence of eternal darkness.

But lest, seeing yourself exposed, you try to break out by replying that you did not say, ‘Evil arose in God’s work because it was made from nothing,’ but rather, ‘Evil could arise because it was made from nothing,’ we must show how much more tightly the snares bind you. If you say that you attributed evil’s possibility, not its necessity, to the powers of that eternal nothing, we reply: the fact that an evil will could arise in a human being is certainly nothing other than free will. An evil will could arise precisely so that a good will could arise too. This is the freedom in which reason exercises itself, on account of which the human being is declared made in God’s image, and by which he excels other creatures (Genesis 1:26–27). If, then, the possibility of an evil will’s arising in a human being is nothing other than freedom of will, and this is so great a thing that its distinction makes him surpass the other living creatures, you who profess that this possibility existed in him not because he was made by God but because he was made from nothing declare, by a new monstrosity of doctrine, that nothing—ancient emptiness—is the cause of so great a good as free will.

To make the matter clear with a brief question: you said, ‘The evil will could arise not because the human being was made by God, but because he was made from nothing.’ This very possibility of the will’s arising, I ask, do you believe it good or evil? That is, do you judge the capacity for a will to arise, which you attributed to nothing, good or utterly evil? If you call it good, then God is not the cause of the good: nothing is. But if, seeing this to be completely insane, you declare it evil—since you say it should be attributed not to God but to nothing—you will testify that we reached no deceitful conclusion against you, but with honest debate overthrew your doctrine’s evil faith. Our result therefore stands unshaken: you and Mani have attributed even the first man’s evil will to the necessity of an eternal origin.
