english: Not content to win in only one way, I will expose the falsehood of the argument whose impiety I have revealed. When you wrote, ‘An evil will could arise in God’s work not because it was made by God, but because it was made from nothing’ (Augustine, Marriage and Desire 2.28.48), you should have seen how powerfully the examples of other creatures argue against you. They too were brought forth from nothing, yet are incapable of an evil will. Indeed, the elements themselves, which truly were made from nothing, can have no consciousness of any will, so as to attest through evil movements the necessity of their origin. Living creatures, however, and the other things filling the world, came forth not from nothing but from something already existing. Where, then, is the power of ancient emptiness that compelled an evil will to exist, when it is clear that no being except a rational creature can sin?

Since this great point was so plain, what persuaded you to believe that the violence of ancient nothing was the cause of an evil will? Certainly it was so that we could understand that you believe everything made from nothing guilty and enslave the whole world to the devil. Since it has become clear to me that your ancient doctrinal agreement remains, I now answer you and Mani together. You ask me, who deny that evil has a nature, to answer if I can: where could the evil will itself arise in the first human being? I reply that you do not understand what you are saying. For will is nothing other than a movement of the mind under no compulsion.

You therefore seek a necessity behind something that cannot exist if it is subject to necessity. If a cause older than the movement itself is assigned to this free movement of the mind, active without compulsion from its origin, the will is not produced at all: it is removed. The very name ‘will’ means nothing other than that the movement does not owe its occurrence to matter. Therefore, when you ask where the will arose, seeking something older than the will itself, you seek not its beginning but its destruction. It cannot be understood to exist if it is attributed either to darkness or to nothing. Nor can that be called will which can exist only as a movement of the mind under no compulsion. If someone compels it, there is indeed a movement, but no will. The will’s force is completed by the definition’s second part: ‘under no compulsion.’ If will is nothing other than a movement of the mind under no compulsion, it is entirely wrong to ask the origin of a thing whose defining condition perishes if something precedes it. Weigh, then, what you ask: ‘Whence could the evil will itself, like an evil tree, arise in the first human being?’ (Augustine, Marriage and Desire 2.28.48). In asking this you confess that will came about through an origin. But will is a movement of the mind under no compulsion. All natural causes compel what follows to exist. If will is compelled by preceding causes, it immediately ceases to be will: by receiving such an origin, it loses its defining condition.

Since will is well defined as ‘a movement of the mind under no compulsion,’ why do you seek earlier causes which the definition of will has excluded? Weigh what will is, and you will stop asking where will comes from. Will is a movement of the mind under no compulsion. If you try to go so much as half a fingernail beyond this, you immediately overthrow what has been established. What does Mani say? ‘This movement arose because the human being was made from the nature of darkness.’ What do you say? ‘Because the human being was made from nothing.’ Thus one says, ‘The will is evil because the human being was made from nothing’; the other, ‘The will is evil in a human being because he was made from darkness.’ Both of you deny what completes the will’s definition: ‘under no compulsion.’ If nothing had as much power as something, and that power compelled this will to exist, it excluded the will’s own condition, expressed as ‘under no compulsion.’

But it has equally driven away evil’s disgrace. What does not come from a free movement of the mind is not sin. Thus, at the expense of truth, all the odium of evil perished. Evil’s nature vanished when the will’s guilt vanished; the will’s guilt vanished when the definition of will was cut apart. It has therefore become clear that the condition of both sin and will is such that, if attributed to preceding causes, it loses both its freedom and its guilt. Where, then, will evil’s nature be, once it is established that no evil exists?

For what is evil, that is, sin? The will to pursue what justice forbids and from which one is free to abstain. What is will itself? A movement of the mind under no compulsion. If sin therefore arose from will, and will from a movement of the mind under no compulsion, neither the condition of nothing nor that of darkness caused this movement to exist. It is compelled by no one precisely so that it can exist under no compulsion. Consequently, there is no natural sin and no original sin. These two names indicate one thing: sin that is not voluntary. But truth has ruled that sin cannot exist unless voluntary. Therefore whoever calls evil what is admittedly innate does not prove that sin exists in nature; he shows himself guilty through a perverse judgment. Here is the answer to what you thought could not be answered. The question you regard as invincible was altogether clever foolishness.

I point out, however, that in your writings you too habitually say darkness is not a creature, but that obscurity remains through the absence of light: darkening is nothing other than the exclusion of brightness. What is excluded you call a creature; what remains you call darkness. This view is indeed widespread among philosophers. I am not now asking whether it should be regarded as true or false. I press this point: you say darkness is nothing other than nothing. Yet you argue that evil arose in a human being, God’s work, because he was made from nothing. You therefore affirm that this nothing was evil’s cause, and you also call this nothing darkness. You thus say the necessity of evil descends from the condition of darkness. Even in this you do not differ from your teacher, since both of you attribute an evil will to eternal darkness.

But just as truth has exposed and overthrown you both, so consideration of our duty requires us to explain what made this now-disarmed question obscure. Everything that occurs is said to arise either from necessity or from possibility. By ‘necessary’ here I mean not what we ordinarily call useful, but what is compelled by stronger causes. We therefore call necessary not what lies within the will’s authority, but what is subject to a force requiring its existence. We call possible what undergoes no necessity on either side, either to exist or not to exist, but in definite ways can exist and can fail to exist. Let our reader hold firmly to what we mean here by necessary and possible.

To begin with great examples: God’s making the world arose from possibility, not necessity. That is, his almighty power made it possible to create what he formed, but not necessary. No one compelled him to make it; he made it because he willed to, and certainly would not have made it had he not willed to. Yet what belonged to the maker as a possibility became a necessity in the work. The world, commanded to exist by the Almighty, did not have the possibility both of existing and not existing: it was compelled to exist, since the Almighty commanded its being.

What came from the creator’s possibility therefore passed into the creature’s necessity. He also made different natures and different species within natures, preserving the order flowing from things’ beginnings: some things were necessary, others possible. Whatever creatures possess naturally, then, they received on the side of necessity.

But what they experience as they go on does not always come from necessity: much comes from possibility. This can be seen in every body, though it would require a longer discussion. Let us give a few examples. Bodies by nature grow together through combination and break apart through division. Those subject to destruction are therefore capable of injury. Their capacity to be wounded comes from necessity; their actually being wounded comes from possibility. Thus the nature of a possibility comes from necessity, although the realization of that possibility is not necessary. For example, a horse, an ox, and similar living creatures have a vulnerable nature, and necessarily possess the capacity for harm. Yet it is not always necessary that they be wounded. If their keepers’ care protects them from blows, they can remain unwounded; if they are not guarded, they can also be wounded. There is therefore a great difference between what arises from possibility and what arises from necessity. Unless this distinction is preserved, countless errors follow.

To make this clear by comparison: some opponents of medicine went astray, arguing that this art has no usefulness. They argue as follows: ‘Does medicine help those who will die or those who will live? If those who will die, it accomplishes nothing; if those who will live, its effort is pointless. Those who were going to die will die despite its labor; those who were going to live could have remained safe without its benefit.’ What a neat and polished conclusion! But medicine’s defenders dissolve it as follows: ‘This art helps neither those who will live nor those who will die by necessity, but those for whom either outcome is possible. Medicine does not help someone who will undoubtedly die, because it cannot make him immortal. Nor does it assist someone who will undoubtedly remain unharmed. It assists someone who can be in danger if untreated, but can be rescued if treated.’ Thus, just as the trained art cannot help someone destined to live or die by necessity, it can help those who may live or die as a matter of possibility. Those earlier critics of medical effort therefore closed with necessity an argument begun from possibility. This form of argument extends to countless matters.

For example, the law forbids homicide. It also forbids providing an occasion of negligence through which people fall into danger, as with a goring bull (Exodus 21:28–32) and the parapets of houses (Deuteronomy 22:8). Someone can say: ‘Does this care help a person who will live or one who will die? If one who will die, it accomplishes nothing; if one who will live, it takes needless precautions’—if these opposite outcomes necessarily follow whether obstacles are present or not. But that is false. Mortals are most rightly protected so that, through the resources of care, they escape what they could have suffered without care. What comes from possibility is therefore one thing; what comes from necessity is another.

Let us now show how these preliminaries help us. God made a human being with free will and a good nature, but one capable of virtues he could acquire for himself through a mind possessing its own freedom. This free will could not stand otherwise than by possessing also the possibility of sinning. A person therefore possesses freedom necessarily, while a particular act of will arises as a possibility. He cannot fail to be free, but cannot be compelled toward either will. A possible effect is thus produced by something necessary. In the possible sphere one can sin; in the necessary sphere one cannot. In the necessary sphere, the one assessed is not the actor but the creator himself: whatever the human being is capable of comes wholly from God. In the possible sphere, however, the actor himself is weighed.
He therefore does both evil and good from his own will. Yet he owes his good to God also, who supplies this side not with a predetermined outcome, but with help.

This distinction has such force that, if through ignorance we conclude in necessity what begins from possibility, every crime returns to God. Mani saw this and invented darkness as sin’s author, since he could not distinguish possibility from necessity. Everything a human being possesses naturally, therefore, he has received on the side of necessity, because he could not be otherwise than he was made.
The evil he does, however, he does from possibility.

Unless the capacity had existed necessarily, its possible result would not have existed. That a person can do evil and good is therefore necessary; his doing evil, however, is owed not to his necessity but to his possibility. Where either side is possible, neither is necessary. Thus sin is nothing other than the will to do what justice forbids and from which one is free to abstain. If will is nothing other than a movement of the mind under no compulsion, then just as God possessed the possibility of making the world, while the world itself received existence under necessity, so something similar is understood in God’s image. A person is not compelled to possess the will he chooses; it comes to him from possibility. The evil he has done, however, carries the necessity of guilt. Thus a crime necessarily incurs its abhorrence, although it arose not from the doer’s necessity but from his possibility. The work of possibility therefore testifies to a free living being.
Blame for this does not pass back to the necessary things, because whatever reaches necessity strikes the creator himself.

Just as what comes from necessity cannot be attributed to my possibility, so what comes from possibility cannot be attributed to necessity. That is, the nature of my body and mind cannot be assigned to my will, as though I were this way because I willed it, since I could not will before I existed. Likewise, the will’s evil cannot be attached to nature, mixing the works of possibility into necessity.

Failing to perceive this subtle distinction, Mani produced swarms of advocates of inherited sin for us. He argues as follows: ‘Where does evil come from? From will, of course. Where does evil will come from?’ He answers, ‘From a human being. Where does the human being come from? Through God.’ He concludes: ‘If evil comes from a human being, and the human being through God, evil therefore comes through God.’ Then, as though religiously avoiding making God criminal, he supplies a nature of darkness to which we should attribute evil. Augustine follows: ‘Where does evil come from? From will. Where,’ he asks, ‘does that will itself come from? From a human being, who is God’s work.’ He concludes: ‘If evil comes from will, will from a human being, and the human being is God’s work, evil therefore comes through God.’ As though trying to solve this without appearing to call God criminal—which his doctrine of transmission affirms—he offers us, in God’s place, an equally violent nothing: that is, darkness, to which we should attribute this evil. ‘For evil arose in a human being,’ he says, ‘not because he was God’s work, but because he was from nothing’ (Augustine, Marriage and Desire 2.28.48).

As though truth could not answer: with what shamelessness does your God first lie that a human being has a will, and then condemn him, when God knows this evil, sin, arose from the necessity of darkness—that is, ancient nothing? I have declined ‘nothing’ through its grammatical cases to display the prowess of the advocate of inherited sin, who places his hope in nothing. But see the weakness of the God he introduces. He could not overcome even nothing. Having made a human being from nothing, he could not free him from the condition of evil that came from nothing. Instead, embittered by the difficulty of affairs, he accuses the human being for his own faults and condemns nothing’s offenses by destroying his own image. Old Mani treats him more kindly, saying that the race of darkness did not ravage him completely. The advocate of inherited sin introduces so great a weakness in God that he invents the claim that God was defeated by nothing.

All who declare war on truth suffer this disgrace. Let us gather our result. The question is where that first evil will arose in a human being. We answer: from a movement of the mind under no compulsion. The objection asks whether it appeared in God’s work. We agree that this is true. We are asked how we do not deny that, although we deny natural sin. We answer: because this sin exists in God’s work from possibility, not necessity. Natural things, then, are necessary; possible things are voluntary.

Consequently, just as we assign sin to a free movement, so we assign nature to God the creator. Human nature is therefore God’s good work. Freedom of will—that is, the possibility either of wrongdoing or of acting rightly—is equally God’s good work. Both come to the human being from necessity; neither is the cause of evil. But those necessary things extend only this far. Will now arises within them, but not from them. They possess the capacity for will, but are not filled with it. They do not produce but receive the differences in moral desert.

The good capacity for evil and good therefore does not compel will to arise, but permits it. No one is good merely because he is endowed with free will: many people are equally free yet utterly evil. Nor is anyone evil because he has free will: many equally share this freedom yet are excellent. A human being is thus neither good nor evil because he is free, but could be neither good nor evil unless he were free. This capacity, indicated by the name freedom, was so established by the supremely wise God that without it there cannot be what is not compelled to exist through it. Its single capacity for opposites protects it from predetermination toward either. That is, it cannot be called the cause or necessity of either an evil or a good will, since it receives both without compelling either to exist. Necessary things therefore have a single course and, as it were, one thread: like geometry’s length without breadth. Its unity cannot be divided. As long as it extends singly, it retains the force of its own nature; but where it meets something divided toward different directions, that necessity immediately ends. That is: the good God made the human being good.

A substance’s beginning, and its good beginning, are governed by the unity of necessity. The human being also receives freedom of will, still within the line of necessity. But here necessary things end; from this point wills divide into opposites. The nature of division does not belong to necessity’s unity. Thus we are compelled to possess the capacity, but not compelled to use that capacity either well or badly. The capacity to sin is therefore capable of good and evil, but voluntary good and evil, because it could not be capable of a person’s own good unless it were capable of wrongdoing too.

The difference between possibility and necessity is as great as that between fullness and emptiness. A capacity is shown empty of the thing it can receive; if it were not empty, it could not receive it. Who would receive what he already had? Necessity, however, indicates not emptiness but fullness. It cannot receive as though empty what it already compels to exist as though full. Necessary things differ from possible things, therefore, as packed things from empty things. The capacity is protected from predetermination toward either quality, for which it is equally capable, precisely by receiving opposites. It possesses in nature the necessary good that reflects its maker’s honor: innocence naturally mixed with no evil, receptive of its own acts, both the distinct merit of good and the blame of evil.

A sinner can wound what comes to him from his own activity; he cannot discolor what he received from God’s work. The valuation of natural goodness therefore remains even in evil people. It will never be evil to have been capable of doing good and evil. But it will not benefit the person who, without actually condemning the institutions of his necessary nature, has compelled them to be of no benefit to himself. In a human being whose freedom is already developed, therefore, when he sins we assign evil to will, but nature to God its creator. If, however, an infant who has no exercise of will and displays nothing except nature’s institutions is said to be full of crime, possessing by necessity the evil another receives by possibility, the one accused as crime’s author is undoubtedly nature’s author.

But why turn to infants, when the Manichaeans’ question does not allow even an adult to sin by will? If evil arose in a human being because he was made from nothing, and he necessarily received his making from nothing, he undoubtedly received evil from necessity, not possibility. Although lengthy argument has destroyed this, let us discuss the same point a little longer, so that repetition makes it increasingly clear. You ask where the evil will itself existed in the first man. I answer: from a movement of the mind under no compulsion. You ask where that movement itself came from. I answer: what are you asking? Where it could come from, or from what it was compelled to exist? If you say, as you also wrote, ‘From what it was compelled to exist,’ I reply that your words are inconsistent and contradictory. You ask who compelled something that cannot exist except under no compulsion. This dissolves through its own contradiction; a question without order has no force.

You therefore ask with great foolishness where the evil will itself comes from. By ‘where,’ you ask not its occasion but its origin, that is, its nature. Yet, as discussed above, if it receives a nature, it loses its own definition, which says ‘under no compulsion’; if it retains its definition, it excludes predetermination by birth. The human being therefore sinned not because he was made from nothing, not because he was made by God, not because he was made from darkness, and not because he was made with free will. He sinned because he willed: that is, he had an evil will because he willed.

Will, then, which is nothing other than a movement of the mind under no compulsion, owes its possibility to nature and its result to itself. It arose within nature, but from possibility, not necessity. If someone says here, ‘But a nature capable of an evil will is evil,’ I answer, ‘But a nature capable of a good will is good.’ It would therefore be called excellent and utterly evil at the same time. Yet the nature of things does not permit one and the same thing at one and the same time to be filled with opposing moral qualities. If it is thought evil because it could do evil, let it be believed good because it could do good. ‘Why,’ he asks, ‘could the nature that did good also do evil?’ I answer: because this good called virtue could not belong to the person as his own unless it were voluntary. It would not be voluntary if it carried the necessity of good; it would have suffered the necessity of good if it had not possessed the possibility of evil. Therefore, to preserve the right of good, the possibility of evil was admitted.

But this can be twisted in the opposite direction: ‘Nature was suited for evil. Since evil could not be voluntary if evil were necessary, the possibility of good was given so that evil could belong to the person as his own.’ This is indeed clever, but insane. Everything is assessed from its better side. Added to this is the dignity of its maker, God: he did not make a free living being for the things he would punish, but gave the possibility of opposites for the things he would reward. Nevertheless, I do not want to fight over this. I allow something to the false objection by declining to settle anything through the maker’s authority. What necessarily follows, however, is that this capacity to do good and evil must be distinguished from the actual result of either will. It is consequently proved to be the necessary cause of neither virtue nor vice.

Even if we insult honorable things by treating their contest with the wicked as grounds to attribute to this capacity neither the merit of a good will nor that of an evil one, it retains the testimony of its freedom: it is innocent because it is full of neither good nor evil—that is, voluntary good or evil. Attribute the possibility of will to nature, then, but attribute neither good nor evil will to nature. The invincible conclusion is that an evil will indeed arose in God’s work, but from possibility, not necessity. This cannot be imputed to the giver of the capacity, but to the one directing that capacity.

Let the discerning reader therefore hold firmly in mind the great difference between what comes from possibility and what comes from necessity. Let him assign all natural things to the necessary, all voluntary things to the possible, and conclude every question on the same side on which it began. If he wanders blindly through both, almost every word plunges him into countless errors. Since this has been made sufficiently clear, you plainly groped in deep darkness when you concluded: ‘Just as evil which existed nowhere could arise in God’s work, so evil already existing passed naturally through God’s work.’ See the error entangling you. You say sin conceived by the first will, which comes from possibility, was changed into something necessary: just as a free movement of the mind could arise, so without a free movement it could pass into the necessity of natural things.

Understand, however, that God is the author of necessary things. If God does in natures what the mind did in sins, he must be guilty in the same way as the one whose will he accuses. Indeed, more guilty: as necessity exceeds possibility, so engendering sin is more criminal than committing it. Although the nature of things does not admit this, I have shown here that your opinion of God is much worse than Mani’s. At least sudden wars mutilated Mani’s God; ancient and multiplied crimes corrupted yours. Consequently, you differ from catholics not merely over a question but over God himself. You do not worship the one whom we venerate in the Trinity as supremely just, supremely powerful, and inviolable.

A matter of will therefore could not pass through nature. We rightly said that the devil’s work is not permitted to pass through God’s work. The devil’s and an evil human being’s work is sin, which can exist in no one without a movement of free will. This work has come and comes to devil and human being from possibility. God’s work, however, is nature, in which a human being exists not by possibility but by necessity. This nature exists for long periods without will, since will’s power is felt at a particular age. As long as nature exists without will, it is solely God’s work; it cannot possess a sin it has not committed. It was therefore said irrefutably that the devil’s work is not permitted to pass through God’s work.

Your statement, ‘The work of God’s work passes through God’s work,’ is as false as it is impious. It amounts to saying, ‘God sins too, because the human being God made sinned.’ For sin exists nowhere except in a human being’s action. When a human being sins, nothing is added to his substance so that sin can be seen projecting there. The evil deed committed from an evil will simply acquires evil desert for the doer too, so that the one who did evil is called evil. Likewise, if your God made evil in his work, nothing is added to his substance, just as nothing is added to a human being’s; but he acquires the most disgraceful desert and is called evil by doing evil. Even then, however, the infant is proved not guilty, since he possesses evil by necessity, whereas even the devil could not be guilty unless he possessed it by possibility. But the true God of Christians does not do evil. Before the determination of its own will, an infant possesses nothing except what God has made within it. No natural sin can therefore exist. Since we have most carefully broken open the ancient error’s caves and nothing about this question remains hidden, let the attentive reader retain the distinction between necessity and possibility. He will laugh at the inventions of Manichaeans and advocates of inherited sin alike.

From the same dullness you also produced this other statement: ‘God creates evil people in the same way as he feeds and nourishes evil people’ (Acts 17:30) (Augustine, Marriage and Desire 2.17.32), because the Gospel says he makes his sun rise over good and evil and sends rain upon just and unjust (Matthew 5:45). What you supposed connected is utterly opposed. God’s feeding even sinners and being kind to the ungrateful and evil (Luke 6:35) testifies to his compassion, not his malice. He does not wish the death of one who dies, but that the person turn back and live (Ezekiel 18:32). He does not quickly punish those who stray. He does this for no other purpose than that his goodness may grant time for repentance. So the apostle says: ‘Or do you not know that God’ (Psalm 119:75)s goodness leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and unrepentant heart, you store up wrath for yourself’ (Romans 2:4–5). He also argues among the Lycaonians and the Areopagites that even in past times of ignorance God did not remove the evidence of his providence (Acts 14:16–17; Acts 17:30): ‘He did not leave himself without testimony, giving rains from heaven and fruitful seasons, filling their hearts with food and gladness’ (Acts 14:17; Latin numbering 14:16) (Acts 14:17).

His raining upon the good and the evil is therefore evidence of his kindness, which bears with and awaits those who stray so that they may finally turn from evil and do good (compare Psalm 34:14; Psalm 37:27; 1 Peter 3:11). Far from wishing evil to occur, he feeds even the ungrateful out of love for human amendment. Against this sign of perfect compassion, however, your statement ‘He creates evil people’ (Psalm 104:24) is evidence of perfect injustice. See how little you know what you are saying: you wanted to prove cruelty by an example of mercy. It is good to feed even evil people, so that they may be corrected if they will. But it is criminal to make infants evil, so that those who cannot will are nevertheless compelled to be wicked. Generosity exercised toward sinners leads away from evils; it does not compel people into evils. Creating evil people does not lead away from the worst things; it drives both the work and its maker into everything abominable.

You are therefore insane when you say, ‘God creates evil’; more insane when you try to affirm it through Gospel testimony, and specifically a testimony containing a great proof of divine goodness. Observe how much more strongly it is now turned back against you. God feeds even evil people so that through his patience he may make them good. Clearly, then, he does not create evil people. But if he creates evil people, he neither loves nor rewards the good, and finally cannot himself possess anything good. For a power that creates not only possible but necessary evils harms more effectively and violently than any evil will. Since this does not fit the Christians’ God—the one called ‘Father of mercy and God of comfort’ (2 Corinthians 1:3), whose judgments are all proclaimed just (Psalm 119:75; LXX/Vulgate 118:75), and who is said to have made everything in wisdom (Psalm 104:24; LXX/Vulgate 103:24)—you, like the Manichaeans, have no share in our understanding of God. Foolish inventions and sins attached to generation have drawn you to worship an entirely different maker, fashioned by Mani’s madness.
